description_full: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (Holdings) Ltd., an investment holding company, engages in shipbuilding activities in the Greater China, Canada, Japan, Italy, Greece, France, Bulgaria, United Kingdom, Singapore, Denmark, Switzerland, and internationally. It operates through Shipbuilding, Shipping, and Others segments. The company offers commercial vessels, such as containerships, multipurpose vessels, oil tankers, bulk carriers, LNG vessels, and other gas carriers. It is also involved in the provision of ship repairing services; production and processing of large-scale steel structures; ship design services; owns and operates a tank terminal; tank related services; and property development. Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (Holdings) Ltd. was founded in 1956 and is based in Jingjiang, China.

financial_summary: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding Holdin is a large-cap industrials business with a $14.1B market cap on $4.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +6.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 54% against a 7% cost of capital — a 47-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 26%.

The business throws off $376M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.52×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 79× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 35% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 32% operating margin runs 23pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.86x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 54% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.42, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $4K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 87% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 34% below its DCF fair value of $5.43, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 26%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $3.82 to $7.97 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/E 10.0 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 0.2 vs 13.4, richer on P/FCF 37.6 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 55.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 2.1% annual cash-flow growth, 8pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 54% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 47pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.46).
It runs a 26% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.52x.
ROE of 27% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 28% last year, worth watching.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.2B.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.8% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 26.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own 35.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 28%.
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 4.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years.
